    58→    pub left_pedal_smoothness: Option<f32>,
    59→    /// T049: Right pedal smoothness percentage
    60→    pub right_pedal_smoothness: Option<f32>,
    61→    /// T130: Left power phase start angle (degrees)
    62→    pub left_power_phase_start: Option<f32>,
    63→    /// T130: Left power phase end angle (degrees)
    64→    pub left_power_phase_end: Option<f32>,
    65→    /// T130: Left power phase peak angle (degrees)
    66→    pub left_power_phase_peak: Option<f32>,
    67→    /// T130: Right power phase start angle (degrees)
    68→    pub right_power_phase_start: Option<f32>,
    69→    /// T130: Right power phase end angle (degrees)
    70→    pub right_power_phase_end: Option<f32>,
    71→    /// T130: Right power phase peak angle (degrees)
    72→    pub right_power_phase_peak: Option<f32>,
    73→}
    74→
    75→impl RideSample {
    76→    /// Create a new ride sample at the given elapsed time.
    77→    pub fn new(elapsed_seconds: u32) -> Self {
    78→        Self {
    79→            elapsed_seconds,
    80→            power_watts: None,
    81→            cadence_rpm: None,
    82→            heart_rate_bpm: None,
    83→            speed_kmh: None,
    84→            distance_meters: 0.0,
    85→            calories: 0,
    86→            resistance_level: None,
    87→            target_power: None,
    88→            trainer_grade: None,
    89→            left_right_balance: None,
    90→            left_torque_effectiveness: None,
    91→            right_torque_effectiveness: None,
    92→            left_pedal_smoothness: None,
    93→            right_pedal_smoothness: None,
    94→            left_power_phase_start: None,
    95→            left_power_phase_end: None,
    96→            left_power_phase_peak: None,
    97→            right_power_phase_start: None,
    98→            right_power_phase_end: None,
    99→            right_power_phase_peak: None,
   100→        }
   101→    }
   102→
   103→    /// Apply cycling dynamics data to this sample.
   104→    pub fn with_dynamics(mut self, dynamics: &crate::sensors::CyclingDynamicsData) -> Self {
   105→        self.left_right_balance = Some(dynamics.balance.left_percent);
   106→        self.left_torque_effectiveness = Some(dynamics.torque_effectiveness.left_percent);
   107→        self.right_torque_effectiveness = Some(dynamics.torque_effectiveness.right_percent);
   108→        self.left_pedal_smoothness = Some(dynamics.smoothness.left_percent);
   109→        self.right_pedal_smoothness = Some(dynamics.smoothness.right_percent);
   110→        // T130: Include power phase data
   111→        if let Some(ref phase) = dynamics.left_power_phase {
   112→            self.left_power_phase_start = Some(phase.start_angle);
   113→            self.left_power_phase_end = Some(phase.end_angle);
   114→            self.left_power_phase_peak = phase.peak_angle;
   115→        }
   116→        if let Some(ref phase) = dynamics.right_power_phase {
   117→            self.right_power_phase_start = Some(phase.start_angle);
   118→            self.right_power_phase_end = Some(phase.end_angle);
   119→            self.right_power_phase_peak = phase.peak_angle;
   120→        }
   121→        self
   122→    }
   123→
   124→    /// Check if this sample has cycling dynamics data.
   125→    pub fn has_dynamics(&self) -> bool {
   126→        self.left_right_balance.is_some()
   127→    }
   128→}

Now I have a thorough understanding of the codebase. The project already has:
- An IPC/daemon architecture with command handlers
- WebSocket streaming server for external displays
- mDNS support for network discovery
- Comprehensive workout/ride control commands
- Ride recording and history storage

I've read the spec and created a comprehensive implementation plan for the **Mobile Companion App** feature. Here's a summary:

## Implementation Plan Overview

### 9 Phases with 55 Subtasks (~110 estimated hours)

| Phase | Name | Subtasks | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| 1 | Backend: Companion Server API | 10 | WebSocket server in Rust with mDNS discovery, PIN auth, metrics streaming, and workout controls |
| 2 | Mobile App: Core Framework | 7 | React Native setup with TypeScript, Zustand state management, WebSocket client |
| 3 | Mobile App: Connection & Auth | 5 | Server discovery, QR scanner, PIN entry, connection persistence |
| 4 | Mobile App: Real-time Dashboard | 7 | Live metrics display (power, HR, cadence), workout interval display |
| 5 | Mobile App: Workout Controls | 5 | Pause/resume/skip/stop buttons with haptic feedback |
| 6 | Mobile App: Ride History | 5 | Paginated ride list, detail view, statistics, offline cache |
| 7 | Mobile App: Settings & Polish | 7 | Settings screen, dark mode, error handling, loading states |
| 8 | Desktop Integration | 4 | Companion panel in desktop UI, QR display, auto-start |
| 9 | Testing & Documentation | 5 | Unit tests, integration tests, user docs, API reference |

### Key Architecture Decisions

- **Backend**: Extends existing Rust infrastructure (tokio-tungstenite, mdns-sd, IPC patterns)
- **Mobile**: React Native with TypeScript for cross-platform iOS/Android support
- **Communication**: WebSocket with JSON messages, PIN authentication, 1Hz metrics streaming
- **Discovery**: mDNS service advertisement (`_rustride._tcp.local`) for auto-discovery on LAN

- ✅ Mobile app connects to desktop app over LAN (Phase 1, 2, 3)
- ✅ Real-time metrics display (power, HR, cadence) (Phase 4)
- ✅ Basic workout controls (pause, resume, skip) (Phase 5)
- ✅ View ride history and statistics (Phase 6)
- ✅ Works on iOS and Android (React Native cross-platform)
